summary: Learners aged 11–12 use the particle model (arrangement, spacing and motion) to EXPLAIN — not just depict — compressibility, relative density, and the ice-water anomaly, keeping particle size and identity fixed. The core activity derives each property from a manipulable particle model: compress each state, count particles per box (a qualitative count-based density proxy for one substance across states) to compare density, and freeze water to watch it lock into an open, spaced lattice that takes up more room (so ice floats). Alternatives include a reveal-panel summary companion, a matching/sequencing check, a predict-observe-explain syringe task, and an optional 3D ice-lattice view. Gas pressure is introduced qualitatively as particle collisions with container walls. Formal kinetic theory and gas laws are deliberately left for later. The density ordering solid > liquid > gas is the typical pattern, with water deliberately treated as the exception (ice less dense than liquid water).
misconceptions: Solids are denser because their particles are 'bigger/heavier', not because they are closer packed.
All solids are denser than their liquids (missing the water/ice anomaly).
Gas pressure comes from particles pushing on each other rather than colliding with the walls.
Particles expand or change on heating rather than moving faster and spreading.

activities.title: Particle explainer: derive compressibility, density and floating ice from a model
steps: Squeeze a piston on a solid, then a liquid, then a gas in a particle simulation; observe that only the gas yields noticeably while a callout shows its empty gaps closing and the close-packed states barely move.
State in your own words why only gases compress much — because only they have large empty spaces between particles to remove, not because particles shrink.

Use a per-box particle counter to compare how many particles fill the same box in each state of the same substance; read off that a gas has far fewer particles in the same space, so it is far less dense. Treat this count as a qualitative, count-based proxy for density (valid for one substance across states), not a literal mass/volume measurement.
Cool liquid water and watch the particles snap into an OPEN, spaced lattice that visibly takes up MORE room; see the resulting ice float on liquid water.
Explain why water is the odd one out — its solid is LESS dense than its liquid because particles lock into an open, spaced structure on freezing — and connect this to why ponds freeze top-down.
Switch to a gas-pressure mode that counts particle hits on the container walls, and describe gas pressure as the result of those collisions with the walls.
activities.insight: The same model — particles of fixed size whose spacing, pattern and motion change — explains compressibility, relative density across states, and the anomalous floating of ice. The explanation is read off the arrangement, not asserted alongside a picture.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: syringe of air vs syringe of water
steps: Before pushing, predict which sealed plunger will push in and how far: a syringe of air (plunger out) or a syringe of water (plunger out), and say WHY in terms of particles.
Push both plungers: observe that air compresses markedly while water barely moves.

Explain the result: in a gas the particles are far apart with empty space between them, so pushing brings them closer (you compress the SPACE, not the particles); in a liquid the particles are already touching (close-packed but disordered), so there is almost no space to remove.

Answer follow-ups: When you squash the air, what gets smaller — the particles or the gaps? Draw it. Using particles, why is a gas much less dense than a solid? What must be different about how particles are arranged in ice so it floats? If it had been oil instead of water, compressible or not, and why the same as water?
activities.insight: The pre-observation reasoning about space between particles — not the observation itself — is intended to be the diagnostic that separates understanding spacing from thinking particles get squashed or the gas 'disappears'.

activities.title: Spacing-explains-property reveal panel (consolidation companion)
steps: Study a contrasting panel showing particle spacing for solid, liquid and gas side by side.
Reveal the 'why it compresses / why it's less dense / why ice floats' flaps and restate each explanation in your own words, pointing to the spacing that causes it.
Open the key panel contrasting ordinary liquid water with its open ice lattice and explain why the open structure makes ice less dense.
activities.insight: Having the three states and their explanations visible together is intended to consolidate that one spacing-based model accounts for all three properties.

activities.title: Match and order: properties to particle explanations
steps: Match each property (compressible, dense, floats) to the particle-arrangement explanation that causes it.
Order the three states by density for a typical substance (solid > liquid > gas) and justify the order from particle spacing.
Then flag water as the deliberate exception: explain why ice (solid water) is LESS dense than liquid water, so it does not fit the usual solid-denser pattern.
Work through this after the simulation so the matching tests explanation-from-model, not recall of labels.
activities.insight: Pairing a property with its spacing-based cause, ranking the typical states by density, and recognising water as the exception checks that the learner reasons from the model rather than reciting a blanket rule.

activities.title: Optional 3D view of the open ice lattice
steps: If the open structure is hard to read in 2D, rotate a 3D packing view of the ice lattice to see how particles sit in a more open, spaced arrangement than in liquid water.
Compare the 3D open lattice with the close-packed arrangement and connect the extra space to lower density.
activities.insight: Density and the ice lattice are genuinely spatial, so seeing the open structure in three dimensions may make the 'more open means less dense' link clearer for some learners.

checkQuestion: You can squash a sealed syringe full of air to half its size, but a sealed syringe full of water barely moves at all. Using what you know about particles, why can you compress the gas but not the liquid? Give me the picture in your head, then the reason.
checkAnswer: In a gas the particles are far apart with empty space between them, so pushing brings them closer — you're compressing the SPACE, not the particles. In a liquid the particles are already touching (close-packed, just disordered), so there's almost no space to remove — hence it barely compresses. The reason rests on SPACING between particles, and on the particles themselves not shrinking.
